check_https_scheme_explanation: HTTPS locks the connection between your visitors and your site, shown as the padlock in the address bar. Without it, browsers label your site as not secure, and anything visitors type, such as a password or card number, can be read on the way. It is a critical check: a site only on http holds the HP down.
check_hsts_explanation: This tells browsers to always open your site over the secure connection, even if someone types or clicks a plain http link. Without it, a visitor on hotel or café Wi-Fi can be quietly pushed to an unprotected copy of your site. Browsers ignore it on a page served over plain http, so it is only checked on https.
check_csp_explanation: A content security policy lists the places your site may load scripts from, so a script an attacker slips in, for example through a plugin, does not run. It only protects if it allows no inline script without a hash or nonce, no script from anywhere, and closes plugins and the base address. Without it, one injected script can read what customers type, including payment details.
check_x_frame_options_explanation: This stops other websites from showing your site inside an invisible frame, by an X-Frame-Options header or a frame-ancestors rule in the content security policy. A rule that allows every site (frame-ancestors *) protects nothing. Without it, a fake page can lay your real buttons under its own and trick visitors into clicking them, for example to confirm an order or change a setting.
check_x_content_type_options_explanation: This tells browsers to treat each file exactly as the type your server says it is. Without it, a browser may guess, and an uploaded image or document that hides code can end up running as a script on your site.
check_referrer_policy_explanation: When a visitor clicks a link to another site, the browser tells that site which page they came from. This setting decides how much of your address goes along. Browsers already send only your domain to other sites when it is missing, so setting it is a hint; a policy that sends the full address (unsafe-url) lets addresses with order numbers, search terms or tokens end up in someone else's logs.
check_permissions_policy_explanation: This switches off browser features your site does not use, such as the camera, microphone or location. If a third-party widget or ad on your page is ever compromised, it then cannot ask your visitors for them. A missing one is a hint, not a hole.
check_coop_explanation: This keeps a page that another site opened from reaching back into yours. It is a newer, optional protection against some cross-site attacks, so a missing one is a small improvement, not an urgent fix.
check_info_leak_explanation: Some servers announce which software and version they run in every response. That is a free hint to attackers, who look up known holes in exactly that version, so hide the version number.
check_cookie_secure_explanation: Cookies remember things such as a logged-in customer, and the Secure flag keeps them off unencrypted connections. Without it, anyone on the same network can copy a login cookie, and browsers refuse a SameSite=None cookie outright. A site that sets no cookies is not checked.
check_cookie_httponly_explanation: The HttpOnly flag hides a cookie from scripts running on the page. Without it, a single malicious script, for example from a compromised plugin, can steal a customer's login session.
check_cookie_samesite_explanation: The SameSite flag stops other websites from sending your cookies along with their own requests. Without it, a page a customer visits elsewhere could act in their name on your site, for example submit a form while they are logged in.
check_mixed_content_explanation: A secure page that loads a script, style or frame over plain http is only as safe as that one file. Anyone on the network can change it, and browsers block it or warn visitors, which can break parts of the page. A page served over plain http is not checked: the HTTPS check covers it.
check_cert_valid_explanation: The certificate proves to browsers that the site really is yours and keeps the connection private. When it is expired, self-signed or issued for another name, browsers put a full-page warning in front of your site, and most visitors leave.
check_ttfb_explanation: How long the server takes to start sending the page, measured from the sitehp.app server. Under 800 ms is good and over 1.8 s is slow, and everything else on the page waits for it. It includes the distance to that server, so take it as a rough guide.
check_compression_explanation: Servers can shrink HTML, CSS and JavaScript before sending them, usually to a quarter of their size. The scanner asks for compression the way a browser does and checks the page and a few of its scripts and stylesheets. Without it every visit downloads several times more than needed, which hurts most on mobile.
check_cache_headers_explanation: Stylesheets and scripts rarely change, so a browser can keep them instead of downloading them on every visit. The scanner looks at a few of them for a Cache-Control lifetime, or at least an ETag or Last-Modified to revalidate. A file marked no-store, or sent without any caching headers, is fetched again each time.
check_http_version_explanation: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 send many files at once over one connection, while HTTP/1.1 makes the browser wait in line or open several. A site passes when it answers with HTTP/2, or advertises HTTP/3. Most hosts and CDNs switch it on with one setting.
check_page_weight_explanation: A heavy page takes long to load on a phone. From the HTML alone the scanner counts its size and how many scripts, stylesheets, images and fonts it points to, and warns over 500 kB or 100 files and fails over 1 MB or 200. Files that scripts load later are not counted.
check_render_blocking_explanation: A script in the head without async or defer makes the browser stop and download it before showing anything. The check warns on one such script or more than four stylesheets, and fails on four scripts. Adding defer to a script usually fixes it.
check_image_formats_explanation: WebP and AVIF pictures are often less than half the size of the same JPEG or PNG. The scanner reads the address of each image on the page and warns when three or more are old formats and fewer than half are modern. SVG images and one or two old ones, like a logo, are fine.
check_lazy_loading_explanation: Images far down the page need not load until the visitor scrolls near them; loading="lazy" does that with one attribute. The scanner takes the first three images in the HTML as the first screen and warns when fewer than half of the rest are lazy. This is an estimate from the HTML order, not from a rendered page.
report_print_hint: Opens your browser's print dialog. Choose Save as PDF as the destination.
report_print_category: {category}: {score} / 100 · {share} % of the HP · {checks} of {total} checks ran
report_print_footer: An automated outside-in check of what a visitor can see. It does not see the source code or the server.
report_fix_first_hint: The checks that would raise your HP the most.
report_categories_hint: Select a category to narrow the checks below.
report_badge_intro: Show your HP on your own site or README. The badge shows only the score, but it links to this report, so anyone who sees it can open the report. It reads Expired once the report is deleted after 30 days.
check_cert_expiry_explanation: Certificates have to be renewed before they run out. Automatic renewal usually happens with about 30 days left, so the check warns only under 14 days and fails under 5. Most certificate outages are a renewal nobody noticed, and on that day every visitor sees a security warning instead of your site.
check_http_redirect_explanation: Someone who types your address without https, or follows an old link, should be sent to the secure version automatically. Without the redirect, they stay on the unprotected page.
check_seo_title_explanation: The page title is the clickable headline in search results and the text on the browser tab. A clear title of about 30 to 60 characters tells people what they will find. Without a good one, search engines make up their own and fewer people click.
check_meta_description_explanation: This is the short text shown under your title in search results, your two-line advert. Write one of about 70 to 160 characters that makes people want to click. Without it, search engines pick a random piece of the page.
check_h1_explanation: The main heading tells visitors and search engines what the page is about, at a glance. A page should have exactly one. Without it, or with several, the topic of the page is less clear and it ranks worse for what you want.
check_viewport_explanation: This tells phones to fit the page to the screen. Without it, phones show a tiny desktop page that people have to pinch and zoom, and Google, which judges the mobile version first, ranks it lower. It should also leave zoom on: user-scalable=no or a maximum-scale below 2 stops people who need larger text from enlarging the page.
check_html_lang_explanation: This states the language the page is written in. Search engines use it to show the page to the right audience, and screen readers use it to read the text in the right voice.
check_canonical_explanation: This names the one official address of a page. Shops often have the same page under several addresses, with filters, tracking codes, or with and without www. Without it, those copies compete with each other in search and none ranks as well as one would.
check_noindex_explanation: A noindex instruction tells Google not to list the page at all. It is often left over from a test version of the site, and it quietly removes the live site from search results.
check_open_graph_explanation: These tags set the title, text and picture shown when someone shares your link on Facebook, LinkedIn, WhatsApp or Slack. Without them, the link appears as a bare address or with a random image, and fewer people click it.
check_open_graph_quality_explanation: Beyond the title, text and picture, a few more tags make a shared link look finished: what kind of page it is, your site's name, its language, a description of the picture for people who cannot see it, and a picture address starting with https:// that apps can fetch. Missing ones are a hint, not a fault.
check_twitter_card_explanation: This controls how your link looks when it is shared on X. Without it, X falls back to the Open Graph tags, so it only matters if you want a different look there.
check_heading_order_explanation: Headings should step down one level at a time, like chapters and sections in a book. Skipping levels blurs the structure of the page for search engines and for visitors who use screen readers.
check_img_alt_explanation: Each image needs a short text description. Search engines use it to understand and show your images, for example product photos in image search, and screen readers read it aloud to blind visitors. Purely decorative images should have an empty description.
check_img_dimensions_explanation: When an image says how wide and tall it is, the browser keeps space for it before it loads. Without that, the text jumps down as images arrive, visitors lose their place or tap the wrong thing, and Google counts the shift against the page. A stylesheet can set the size too, which the scanner cannot see, so a gap is only a hint.
check_favicon_explanation: The favicon is the small icon on browser tabs, in bookmarks and next to your site in some search results. Without it, visitors see a blank placeholder, and the site looks unfinished next to others.
check_json_ld_explanation: Structured data describes the page in a form search engines read directly, such as a product with its price or your company, and can earn richer search results. Each item needs a @type; a block with an error or without a type is silently ignored. Google no longer shows how-to results, and question-and-answer ones only for government and health sites.
check_hreflang_explanation: If your site exists in several languages, these links tell search engines which version to show to whom, for example Czech to people in Czechia. When they are wrong or one-sided, search engines ignore them and may show the wrong language. A site in one language is not checked.
check_robots_txt_explanation: robots.txt is a small file that tells search engines which parts of the site they may visit. A missing one is harmless (search engines then visit everything), but one that answers with a server error makes Google stay away until it recovers.
check_robots_allows_page_explanation: The rules in robots.txt must let search engines fetch this page. A leftover rule such as Disallow: / keeps the whole site out of Google, and a blocked page also hides its own noindex from search engines, so it can still be listed without a description. It is a critical check: a blocked page holds the HP down.
check_sitemap_xml_explanation: A sitemap is a list of the pages you want search engines to find. It helps new pages and products show up in search sooner. A broken or empty sitemap is ignored.
check_sitemap_in_robots_explanation: Naming your sitemap in robots.txt is the one place every search engine looks for it, with no account or setup needed. Without it, search engines that you have not told about it may never find it.
check_sitemap_urls_explanation: The pages your sitemap lists should open normally. The scanner tries a few of them. A sitemap full of missing or redirected pages makes search engines trust it less and visit your site less often.
check_redirect_chain_explanation: An old address should lead to the page in one or two jumps, such as from http to https and then to the www or bare name. Longer chains slow visitors down and waste the time search engines spend on your site. A temporary redirect to another site keeps the old address in search results instead of the new one.
check_soft_404_explanation: A page that does not exist should say so with the error code 404. If it pretends to be a normal page instead, search engines may index thousands of empty pages and judge the whole site as lower quality.
check_canonical_host_explanation: Your site should open under one name only, for example always with www or always without, with the other sending visitors over. If both work on their own, search engines see two copies of your site and split its ranking between them.
report_failed: The scan could not be completed.
report_failed_blocked_address: This address can't be scanned: it points to a private or internal network. Use the public address of a website.
report_failed_unreachable: The website could not be reached. Check the address and try again.
report_failed_timeout: The website took too long to answer.
report_failed_too_many_redirects: The website redirects too many times.
report_failed_tls_error: The website's security certificate could not be verified, so the page could not be loaded.
report_failed_invalid_response: The website sent a response that could not be read.
report_failed_internal_error: Something went wrong on my side. Try again.
check_http_status_explanation: The page should answer with a success code. A page that answers with an error cannot be found, ranked or used, so visitors and search engines turn away. It is a critical check: an error page holds the HP down, because the rest of the page cannot be judged.
home_trust: Free · No sign-up · Results in seconds
home_check_intro: {count} checks in {categories} categories, run from the outside, the way a visitor, a search engine or an AI agent sees your site.
home_check_security_body: HTTPS and certificate, security headers, cookie flags and mixed content: what decides whether browsers trust your site.
home_check_seo_body: Titles and descriptions, headings, canonical and indexing rules, robots.txt and sitemap, redirects and social previews: what decides whether search engines find and show your pages.
home_check_speed_body: Time to first byte, compression, caching, HTTP version, page weight, render-blocking files and images: what makes a page feel slow. Estimated from the HTML and the server's answers, not measured in a real browser.
home_check_next_body: Cookie banners, trackers set before consent and a link to the privacy policy are on the list for later. I add a category when it is good enough to rely on.
home_how_1_body: Type any public website. No account, nothing to install.
home_how_2_body: The scanner requests the page from the outside, as a crawler does, under its own name, and runs the checks. Nothing on your site is changed.
home_how_3_body: You get a score and a list ranked by how many HP each fix is worth, with the effort it takes.
home_sample_title: Explained for people, not only for developers
home_sample_body: Every finding says what it is, what was found on your page, why it matters and what fixing it is worth. Developers get the measured values and a copy-ready fix one step deeper.
home_trust_title: Built to be safe to use
home_trust_1_body: You do not need an account to scan a site or read its report.
home_trust_2_body: The scanner reads what any visitor can read. It never logs in, submits forms or tries to break in.
home_trust_3_body: A report is reachable only through its link and is kept out of search engines.
home_trust_4_body: sitehp.app checks cookie flags but never stores cookie values. A report keeps the page title, description, main heading and response headers, and is deleted after 30 days.
home_faq_1_a: Yes. Scanning a site and reading its report is free and needs no account.
home_faq_2_q: Can I scan a site that is not mine?
home_faq_2_a: Yes. The scanner only requests what any visitor's browser can request, and scans are rate limited so nobody's site is overloaded.
home_faq_3_q: What does the HP score mean?
home_faq_3_a: It is the share of points kept after the checks, weighted by how serious each one is. Every lost point leads to one finding. The weights are still being tuned on real sites.
home_faq_4_q: Does it tell me how to fix things?
home_faq_4_a: Yes. Almost every finding has step-by-step fixes with a snippet to copy: one for any site and, where the steps differ, for nginx, Apache, Next.js, WordPress, Shopify or Cloudflare. The platform the scanner recognises opens first.
home_faq_5_a: No. It only sees what is visible from the outside. For a full review of your code and setup, you need people who can look inside.
home_faq_6_a: sitehp.app is an independent project built and run by {name}.

footer_brand_text: A free website health check. It looks at your site from the outside and tells you what to fix first.
seo_about_title: About the free website health check
seo_about_description: sitehp.app is a free website health check, built and run as an independent project. Learn why it was built, what it checks and how it works.
seo_blog_title: Blog: how website health checks work
seo_blog_description: Articles from the maker of sitehp.app: how the scanner works, what each check means and how to fix what a report finds on your site.
about_lead: sitehp.app is a free website health check. It looks at your site from the outside, scores it from 0 to 100 and tells you what to fix first, in plain language.
about_why_body: When I build a new website or application, I want one scanner that goes through everything that matters to me on a new site: security, SEO, speed and readiness for AI agents. I could not find one that did all of it in one place and explained it plainly, so I built it. It finds the problems in seconds and says what to fix first.
about_can_intro: {count} checks in {categories} categories, run from the outside in a few seconds. This is what you get from one scan:
about_can_1_title: One score, and where it comes from
about_can_1_body: A HP score from 0 to 100 for the whole site, with a score for security, SEO, speed and agent readiness beside it, so you see which part pulls it down.
about_can_2_title: Fixes in the order that pays
about_can_2_body: Every finding says what it is, what was found on your page, why it matters, how many HP fixing it is worth and roughly how long it takes. The cheapest wins come first, and almost every one comes with a step-by-step fix.
about_can_3_title: Honest about what it could not see
about_can_3_body: A check that could not run, because of a firewall, a cookie wall or an error page, is marked as not checked and left out of the score.
about_can_4_title: A report you can pass on
about_can_4_body: Each scan has its own link with a preview image of its score. Export the findings as PDF, JSON, or Markdown written for an AI coding assistant, with the fix steps and links to the documentation. A badge with your score can go on your own site.
about_can_5_body: Start a new scan from the report as soon as you have changed something, and see the score move.
about_how_1_body: The scanner requests pages from the outside, as a crawler does, under its own user agent, and reads the answer. It never logs in, submits forms or tests for weaknesses.
about_how_2_body: A check that cannot run is marked as not checked, and the score is based on what did run. I say so instead of guessing.
about_how_3_body: Each finding says what it is, why it matters and what fixing it is worth. The technical detail is one step deeper, never removed.
about_not_body: It is not a penetration test, not a keyword research tool and not a replacement for a human audit. It only sees what is visible from the outside.
about_operator_body: sitehp.app is built and run by {name} as an independent project.
schema_operator_description: {name} builds and runs sitehp.app, a free website health check.
report_skipped_not_run: The scan ended before this check ran.
report_skipped_blocked: The site turned the scanner away (access denied or too many requests), so this could not be checked.
report_skipped_consent_wall: The site sent the scanner to its cookie consent page instead of the page itself, so the page's content was not judged.
report_skipped_check_error: The check hit an unexpected problem and was skipped. The score does not count it.
report_skipped_compressed: The file is compressed, and the scanner can only read plain text for now.
report_skipped_error_page: The page answered with an error, so its content was not judged as the site's own.
report_skipped_no_certificate: No secure connection answered, so there is no certificate to look at.
report_skipped_no_headings: The page has no headings, so there is no order to check.
report_skipped_no_robots: There is no robots.txt to look in.
report_skipped_no_sample: There was no list of pages in a sitemap to try.
report_skipped_not_html: The address does not return a web page (HTML), so it has no tags to read.
report_skipped_too_deep: The page's HTML is nested deeper than a browser builds it (over 512 levels), so it was not read.
report_skipped_truncated: The page is large and the scanner read only its beginning, which did not show this.
report_skipped_unreachable: The file could not be fetched from the site.
report_skipped_other: This check did not run, and the score does not count it.
seo_methodology_description: How sitehp.app turns dozens of checks into one 0–100 HP score: the weights, the rules and every check a scan runs.
method_lead: The HP score is a number from 0 to 100 that sums up {count} checks. Here is exactly how it is calculated, what is checked and what is still to come. Nothing on this page is hidden in the score.
method_step_1_body: Passed, warning, failed or not checked. A check that cannot run, for example because the page could not be read, is marked not checked and left out of the score instead of being guessed.
method_step_2_body: The weight is its severity. A failed check loses its full weight, a warning loses half, a passed check loses nothing.
method_step_3_title: A category keeps a share of its points
method_step_3_body: Within one category, the score is the share of the weighted points that were kept. A category with no check that ran is left out, and the others share its weight.
method_step_4_title: Categories add up to the HP
method_step_4_body: The category scores are averaged with the weights below, and the result is rounded to a whole number.
method_step_5_title: A critical failure holds the score down
method_step_5_body: If a critical check fails, the HP cannot be higher than {cap}, however well the rest does. The critical checks are an untrusted certificate, a site only on http, a page that answers with an error, and a page that search engines are told to ignore or are not allowed to fetch. A site like that is not in good health.
method_severity_caption: Weight of a check by severity
method_category_weights_body: Security, SEO, speed and agent readiness are live. Privacy is planned and already has a weight, so adding it later changes the model in a way that is written down, not by surprise. Until it arrives, the live categories share the whole HP, so today each counts for the share shown next to it.
method_limits_title: When there is no score, or less of one
method_limits_blocked: If the site answers the scanner with 401, 403 or 429, or with a bot challenge (Cloudflare, AWS WAF, Imperva), a firewall turned it away. The report shows no score instead of grading a block page.
method_limits_skipped: A check that could not run, or one that does not apply to the site (cookie flags on a site without cookies, language versions on a site in one language), says so and says why. It is left out of the score, so a site gains nothing from it; each category shows how many of its checks ran.
method_limits_gain: Each finding shows the HP you gain by fixing it: the score recomputed as if that one check passed. While a critical failure holds the score at its cap, a fix elsewhere gains only up to the cap, so it shows no gain when the rest already scores above it.
method_limits_version: Weights can change. Each change gets a new model version, so a score is only compared with scores from the same version.
method_checks_intro: Every check below runs on every scan, from the outside, the way a visitor or a search engine sees your site. The scanner requests pages from the outside, as a crawler does, identified by its own user agent, and reads what comes back without running the page's scripts. The speed checks are estimates from the HTML and the server's answers, not a measurement in a real browser.
method_cta_title: See it on your own site
method_cta_body: It takes a few seconds, needs no sign-up and the checks above run for real.
check_link_headers_title: Agent links in the Link header
check_link_headers_explanation: The Link header of a page can point an agent to your API catalog, your service description or your documentation (RFC 8288). It is a bonus signal: a site without one is not penalised. The check looks for the api-catalog, service-desc, service-doc and describedby relations.
check_api_catalog_explanation: An API catalog at /.well-known/api-catalog (RFC 9727) is a JSON list that tells an agent which APIs your site offers and where they are described. It is a bonus signal: most sites have no API, and a site without one is not penalised. A file that is there but is not a valid linkset only warns.
check_oauth_resource_explanation: A protected resource can say which authorization server an agent should use to get access to it, at /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource (RFC 9728). It is a bonus signal and most sites do not need it. A document without the required resource field only warns.
check_a2a_agent_card_explanation: An Agent Card at /.well-known/agent-card.json tells other agents what your own agent can do, using the A2A protocol. It is a bonus signal for sites that run an agent, and a site without one is not penalised. A card without a name or a list of skills only warns.
report_skipped_not_offered: The site does not publish this. It is a bonus signal, so the score is not lowered.
finding_api_catalog_invalid: Your /.well-known/api-catalog answers, but it is not a valid linkset (a JSON object with a linkset list).
finding_api_catalog_empty: Your API catalog is valid but lists no APIs.
finding_oauth_resource_invalid: Your protected resource metadata has no resource field.
finding_a2a_invalid: Your agent card answers, but it has no name or no list of skills.
method_limits_bonus: Some checks are bonus signals, such as an API catalog or an A2A agent card. A site that publishes one gains a little. A site that does not is not penalised: the check is left out of the score. A file that is there but wrong only warns.
check_llms_txt_explanation: llms.txt is a short file that gives AI assistants such as ChatGPT or Claude an overview of your site and links to its most useful pages. It is a proposal, not a standard, and no search engine requires it. Without it, an assistant has to guess its way around your site.
check_markdown_negotiation_explanation: Web pages carry menus, scripts and styling that AI agents have to wade through. A site can offer the same page as clean text when an agent asks for it, which the agent reads faster and more accurately. Without it, agents read the full page and may miss the point.
check_ai_crawlers_explanation: AI search tools and assistants send their own robots to read your pages when someone asks about you. If robots.txt shuts them out, or its Content-Signal says search=no or ai-input=no, those assistants cannot read or recommend your site. Keeping out robots that only collect training data is a legitimate choice, so it is only reported.
check_content_in_html_explanation: Most AI agents, and some search robots, read the page your server sends without running its scripts. If your text only appears after JavaScript runs, they see an empty page and cannot summarize, quote or recommend you.
report_skipped_robots_error: robots.txt answered with a server error, so its rules for AI crawlers are unknown.
home_check_agent_body: Whether an AI agent can read and use your site: llms.txt, Markdown versions of your pages, the rules for AI crawlers in robots.txt and content that is in the HTML without scripts. Bonus signals such as an API catalog or an A2A agent card add a little when you publish them and never lower the score.
report_connection_lost: Lost the live connection to this scan. Still trying, less and less often.
report_follow_ended: This scan can no longer be followed live. Reload the page to see where it got to.
report_not_found_body: There is no report at this address. Reports are kept for 30 days and then deleted. Scan the site again to get a fresh one.
scan_form_no_js: Scanning needs JavaScript. Turn it on in your browser to scan a website.
report_skipped_meta_refresh: The page sends visitors on with a meta refresh instead of showing its own content, so its content was not judged.
report_skipped_login_wall: The site sent the scanner to a login page instead of the page itself, so the page's content was not judged.
report_older_model: This report was scored with scoring model version {version}; the current one is {current}. The HP is shown as it was given, without the breakdown by area, which today's weights would split differently. Scan again to see the site under the current model.
report_banter_10: Poking a page that doesn't exist…
blog_lead: Notes on how sitehp.app works, what it checks and why, written by the person who builds it.
